title: Chapter 47 — The Mat-Maker
paragraphs: It was a cloudy, sultry afternoon. The seamen were lazily lounging about the decks or gazing vacantly over the rail into the lead-colored waters. Queequeg and I were quietly weaving what is called a sword-mat, to use as an additional lashing for our boat. So still and subdued was the whole scene, and yet somehow so full of anticipation, and such a spell of daydreaming lurked in the air, that each silent sailor seemed dissolved into his own invisible self.

I was Queequeg's attendant, or page, while he was busy at the mat. As I kept passing the filling, or woof, of marline back and forth between the long yarns of the warp, using my own hand as the shuttle, and as Queequeg, standing sideways, every now and then slid his heavy oaken sword between the threads and, idly looking off at the water, carelessly and unthinkingly drove every yarn home — I say, so strange a dreaminess reigned then over all the ship and all the sea, broken only by the intermittent dull sound of the sword, that it seemed as if this were the Loom of Time, and I myself a shuttle mechanically weaving and weaving away at the Fates. There lay the fixed threads of the warp, subject to only one single, ever-returning, unchanging vibration, and that vibration just enough to allow other threads to be interwoven crosswise with its own. This warp seemed necessity; and here, I thought, with my own hand I ply my own shuttle and weave my own destiny into these unalterable threads. Meanwhile Queequeg's impulsive, indifferent sword sometimes hit the woof slantwise, or crookedly, or strongly, or weakly, as the case might be, and by this difference in the concluding blow produced a corresponding contrast in the final look of the finished fabric. This savage's sword, I thought, which in the end shapes and fashions both warp and woof — this easy, indifferent sword must be chance — yes, chance, free will, and necessity, in no way incompatible, all working together, interwoven. The straight warp of necessity, not to be swerved from its ultimate course — its every alternating vibration, indeed, only tending toward that; free will, still free to ply her shuttle between given threads; and chance, though restrained in its play within the straight lines of necessity, and directed sideways in its motions by free will — though thus hemmed in by both, chance rules each of them by turns, and strikes the last, shaping blow at events.

We were weaving and weaving away like this when a sound made me start — a sound so strange, so drawn-out, so musically wild and unearthly, that the ball of free will fell from my hand, and I stood staring up at the clouds that voice had dropped from like a wing. High up in the crosstrees was that mad Gay Header, Tashtego. He was leaning eagerly forward, his hand stretched out like a wand, and in brief, sudden bursts he kept up his cries. Of course, that same sound was perhaps ringing out at that very moment all over the seas, from hundreds of whalemen's lookouts perched just as high; but few of those lungs could have given that familiar old cry such a marvelous cadence as Tashtego the Indian's did.

As he stood hovering over you, half-suspended in air, peering so wildly and eagerly toward the horizon, you would have thought him some prophet or seer beholding the shadows of Fate, and announcing their coming with those wild cries.
"There she blows! There! There! There! She blows! She blows!"
"On the lee beam, about two miles off! A school of them!"
The Sperm Whale blows as a clock ticks, with the same unwavering and reliable regularity. And by this the whalemen distinguish this fish from other species of his kind.
"There go flukes!" was now the cry from Tashtego, and the whales disappeared.
Dough-Boy hurried below, glanced at the watch, and reported the exact minute to Ahab.

The ship was now kept away from the wind, and she went gently rolling before it. Since Tashtego reported that the whales had gone down heading to leeward, we confidently expected to see them again directly ahead of our bows. For that singular cunning the Sperm Whale at times shows — when, sounding (diving deep) with his head in one direction, he nevertheless mills round while hidden beneath the surface and swiftly swims off the opposite way — this deceitfulness of his could not be at work now; for there was no reason to suppose that the fish Tashtego had seen had been alarmed in any way, or indeed knew we were anywhere near. One of the men chosen as shipkeepers — that is, those not assigned to the boats — had by this time relieved the Indian at the mainmast head. The sailors at the fore and mizzen had come down; the line tubs were fixed in their places; the cranes were thrust out; the mainyard was backed; and the three boats swung over the sea like three samphire baskets over high cliffs. Outside the bulwarks their eager crews clung to the rail with one hand, while one foot was poised expectantly on the gunwale. That is how the long line of a man-of-war's men looks when they are about to throw themselves aboard an enemy's ship.

But at that critical moment a sudden shout went up that pulled every eye away from the whale. Startled, everyone stared at dark Ahab, who stood surrounded by five dusky phantoms that seemed to have just taken shape out of the air.
